headings_not_bold.problem: This code uses a heading incorrectly for visual effect only.
headings_not_bold.solution:
Solution 1

Use CSS properties to create text that looks like a heading when you only need visual styling, not semantic heading structure. This preserves the document's proper heading hierarchy while achieving the desired visual effect.
Code example: 

<style>
  .fake_heading{
    font-size: 20px;
    font-weight: bold;
  }
</style>
<div class="fake_heading">
    UsableNet AQA
</div>

Solution 2

Mark important text with the <strong> element instead of styling it to look like a heading. The <strong> element provides semantic meaning that indicates the text has strong importance, while heading elements should only be used for actual headings that structure your document.
Code example: 

<strong>Do not feed the animals!</strong>

formatting_with_spaces.problem: This content improperly uses white spaces characters to create multiple columns or format tables in plain text.
formatting_with_spaces.solution:
Use proper table markup to present tabular information. This preserves relationships within the information even when users cannot see the table or when the presentation format changes. Use the <table> element with the child elements <tr>, <th>, and <td> to make these relationships clear to assistive technologies. Avoid techniques like inserting white space characters (such as the tab character) to create columns or using the <pre> element for tables. These methods are purely visual, and the logical relationships between data are lost when users cannot see the visual layout or when the presentation changes.

       activities from Monday to Friday, 
       organized by time slots in the morning.">

  <tr>
    <td> </td>
    <th>Monday</th>

    <th>Wednesday</th>
    <th>Thursday</th>
    <th>Friday</th>

    <td> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th>10:00-11:00</th>
    <td> </td>
    <td>Linear Algebra</td>

    <td>Statistics</td>
    <td>Computer Networks</td>

missing_strong.problem:

User agents can then make the structure perceivable to users, for example by using a different visual presentation for different types of structures or by using a different voice or pitch in auditory presentation. For example, <strong> element indicate structural emphasis.

deployment, and that's what makes him a 
<strong>great</strong> developer.

color_in_images.problem:
The image conveys information through color alone, without providing an alternative visual indicator (such as
        patterns, textures, labels, or symbols) that is visible on the page. This makes the information inaccessible to

color_in_images.solution:

<h1>Subway</h1>

     alt="UsableNet city subway map">

  <p>Legend:</p>
  <ul>
    <li class="line red-line">
      Red Line: Striped

    <li class="line blue-line">
      Blue Line: Dotted
    </li>
    <li class="line green-line">
      Green Line: Dashed
    </li>
  </ul>
  <p>
    Lines differ by color 
    <strong>and pattern</strong> 
    for clarity.
  </p>
</div>

meaningful_sequence.solution:
Solution 1

Position content based on structural markup. You can enhance visual appearance with style sheets while maintaining meaningful presentation when style sheets are not applied. CSS2 positioning properties let you display content at any position on users' viewports. Using structural elements ensures that you can still determine the meaning of the content when styling is not available.
Code example: 

<style>
  .container {
    position: absolute;
    top: 4rem;
    left: 3rem;
  }
  .section {
    background-color: #f0f8ff;
    color: #003366;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    font-size: 1.2rem;
    top: 2rem;
  }
  .left {
    position: absolute;
    margin: 0;
    width: 18rem;
    left: 1rem;
  }
  .right {
    position: absolute;
    margin: 0;
    width: 18rem;
    left: 20rem;
  }
  .row1 {
    top: 6rem;
  }
  .row2 {
    top: 7rem;
  }
  .row3 {
    top: 8rem;
  }
</style>
...

  <dl>
    <dt class="left section">
      Student Services
    </dt>
    <dd class="left row1">
      Advising
    </dd>
    <dd class="left row2">
      Counseling
    </dd>
    <dd class="left row3">
      Career Center
    </dd>
    <dt class="right section">
      Academic Departments
    </dt>
    <dd class="right row1">
      Biology
    </dd>
    <dd class="right row2">
      History
    </dd>
    <dd class="right row3">
      Computer Science
    </dd>
  </dl>

Order the content in a meaningful sequence. This technique ensures that the order of content presented to assistive technologies allows users to make sense of the content. Some techniques let you render the content visually in a meaningful sequence even if this differs from the order in which you encode the content in the underlying source file.
Code example: 

...
<style>
  #nav {
    float: left;
    width: 8em;
    padding: 0.5em;
    list-style: none;
    background: #444;
  }
  #nav a {
    display: block;
    color: white;
    text-decoration: none;
  }
  #description {
    margin-left: 10em;
  }
</style>
...
<h1>Wildlife Gallery</h1>
<ul id="nav">
  <li><a href="#">Birds</a></li>
  <li><a href="#">Mammals</a></li>
  <li><a href="#">Reptiles</a></li>
</ul>
<div id="description">
  <h2>Red Fox</h2>
  <p>
    <img src="fox.jpg" 
         alt="Red fox in snowy forest">
  </p>
  <p>
    A red fox caught mid-step during snowfall 
    in northern Europe.
  </p>
</div>
...

Make the DOM order match the visual order. Authors can use CSS to display content in any visual presentation, independent of how it is ordered in the source code. Each order may be meaningful in itself but may confuse assistive technology users. This could happen when users switch off your specified presentation, access the content directly from the source code (such as with a screen reader), or interact with the content using a keyboard. If a blind user who reads the page with a screen reader that follows the source order works with a sighted user who reads the page in visual order, they may encounter confusion when they find information in different orders. A user with low vision who uses a screen magnifier in combination with a screen reader may feel confused when the reading order appears to skip around on the screen. A keyboard user may have trouble predicting where focus will go next when the source order does not match the visual order.
Code example: 

...
<style>
  nav {
    background: #ccc;
    padding: 0.5em;
  }
  main {
    padding: 1em;
  }
</style>
...
<header>
  <h1>Daily Globe</h1>
</header>
<nav>
  <a href="#">Home</a> |
  <a href="#">Politics</a> |
  <a href="#">Tech</a>
</nav>
<main>
  <h2>Breaking News</h2>
  <p>
    Major updates from around the world...
  </p>
</main>
...

text_with_background.problem: A background image or gradient causes insufficient contrast between the text and its background.
text_with_background.solution:
Solution 1

Make sure a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (or 3:1 for large text) exists between the foreground and background colors.

If the background or text is not a uniform color (i.e., a textured background image), make sure each letter has sufficient contrast with its immediate background (at least 4.5:1 for standard text or 3:1 for large text). Also ensure that the contrast remains sufficient when the text position changes, such as when users resize the browser window or zoom the page.

Solution 2

Position text to avoid overlapping with background images whenever possible, ensuring sufficient contrast with the background. When background images are necessary, verify that the contrast ratio between text and the background image meets accessibility standards: a minimum of 4.5:1 for standard text and 3:1 for large text.

explicit_svg_alt_meaningful.problem: This <svg> element lacks proper alternative text content. Assistive technologies cannot provide useful information to users when the alternative text fails to match the SVG's actual purpose.
explicit_svg_alt_meaningful.solution:
Solution 1

Use WAI-ARIA aria-label to create labels for objects. The WAI-ARIA aria-label attribute gives objects a text label. Assistive technologies read this WAI-ARIA aria-label text aloud, so users understand what they are encountering.
Code example: 

<svg role="img" aria-label="Contact us">
    …
</svg>

Note

Include any important words from the image in your alternative text. This lets the alternative text serve the same purpose as the image:

  • Focus on what the image means or why it matters in its context, not necessarily what it shows visually.
  • Keep your alternative text short while still giving users all the important information they need.
  • If the image contains text (i.e. a quote or important words), include that exact text in your alternative text.
    Note: it might be still violating Success Criterion 1.4.5.
Solution 2

Set a non-empty valid value to the WAI-ARIA aria-labelledby attribute. This attribute connects an element to text somewhere else available on the page. Set the WAI-ARIA aria-labelledby attribute to the id of the element containing the alternative text. Assistive technologies will use the text from that other element as the alternative text. Remember also to set the appropriate role, such as role="image".
Code example: 

<svg role="img" aria-labelledby="rating_id">
    ...
</svg>
<div id="rating_id" class="sr-only">
    Rating: 4 of 5
</div>

Note

  • Focus on what the image means or why it matters in its context, not necessarily what it shows visually.
  • Keep your alternative text short while still giving users all the important information they need.
  • If the image contains text (i.e. a quote or important words), include that exact text in your alternative text.
    Note: it might be still violating Success Criterion 1.4.5.

input_without_computed_name.problem: The form control does not have an accessible name and assistive technologies cannot convey its purpose.
input_without_computed_name.solution:
Solution 1

Use <label> elements to associate text labels with form controls and provide accessible names. Attach explicitly a label to a specific form control by using the for attribute. The for attribute value must match the id attribute value of the form control. The <label> element content must be meaningful and the id value must be unique on the web page.
Code example: 

<label for="fn">First name</label>
<input type="text" name="first_name" id="fn">

Note

Always make the label - whether or not it is an HTML <label> element - visible, unless the form control's purpose is clearly shown by the layout.

Solution 2

Use <label> elements to associate text labels with form controls and provide accessible name. You can associate a label with a form control by wrapping the <input> element inside the <label> element. Make sure the <label> element contains meaningful text.
Code example: 

<label>
  <span>First name</span>
  <input type="text" name="first_name">
</label>

Note

Always make the label - whether or not it is an HTML <label> element - visible, unless the form control's purpose is clearly shown by the layout.

Solution 3

If you cannot use a <label> element, use the WAI-ARIA aria-labelledby attribute instead. Set the WAI-ARIA aria-labelledby value to match the id of the element that describes this form control. Make sure the describing element contains meaningful text.

<input aria-labelledby="fn"
       type="text" name="first_name">

Code example:

<input aria-label="First name" 
       type="text" name="first_name" >

js_refresh.problem:
The intent of this rule is to ensure that users with disabilities have sufficient time to interact with web
        content whenever possible.
js_refresh.solution:
Solution 1

Provide a way for users to turn the time limit off. Make sure the mechanism for turning off the time limit can be completed without a time limit itself and before the time limit for the page expires. Place this mechanism at or near the top of the page so that people with a wide range of disabilities can find and activate it quickly.

Solution 2

Provide users with a means to set the time limit to 10 times the default time limit. Use a mechanism such as a preference setting or a control on the page that lets users change the time limits to at least 10 times the default time limit. Preferably, the mechanism would have a variable adjustment that lets users change the time limit to any value in its range, but can also provide ways to change the time limit by discrete increments. Users should change the time limit at the beginning of their session, before any activity that has a time limit.

resizing_page.problem: Avoid using CSS settings that prevent text resizing.
resizing_page.solution:
Solution 1

Define the size of text containers using em units. This lets user agents resize containers in line with text size settings.
Code example: 

input.search-field {
  font-size: 1rem;
  width: 20em;
}

Solution 2

Set font sizes using percentages. When you define a font-size on the <body> element, other elements inherit it unless overridden by more specific selectors.
Code example: 

<style>
  strong {
    font-size: 120%;
  }
</style>

<h1>
  Protecting your <strong>account</strong>.
</h1>
<p>
  It is <strong>crucial</strong> to use:
</p>
<ol>
  <li>strong passwords</li>
  <li>enable two-factor authentication</li>
</ol>

Solution 3

Use named font sizes. These values help the user agent scale fonts relative to the inherited size.
Code example: 

<style>
  strong {
    font-size: larger;
  }
</style>

<h1>
  Protecting your <strong>account</strong>.
</h1>
<p>
  It is <strong>crucial</strong> to use:
</p>
<ol>
  <li>strong passwords</li>
  <li>enable two-factor authentication</li>
</ol>

Solution 4

Use em units for font sizes. The em unit is relative to the font, so it scales when the font size changes. When you define a font-size on the <body> element, other elements inherit it unless overridden by more specific selectors.
Code example: 

<style>
  strong {
    font-size: 1.5em;
  }
</style>

<h1>
  Protecting your <strong>account</strong>.
</h1>
<p>
  It is <strong>crucial</strong> to use:
</p>
<ol>
  <li>strong passwords</li>
  <li>enable two-factor authentication</li>
</ol>

Solution 5

Use a liquid layout to design your pages. This means that page sections grow or shrink with the text and move to fit smaller or larger screens. Even if the layout changes, the reading order and the position of content stay clear and consistent. Liquid layouts help your site work better on all devices and for people who need larger text.
Code example: 

...
<style>
  body {
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    margin: 1em;
  }
  .wrapper {
    overflow: hidden;
    margin-bottom: 1em;
  }
  .box {
    float: left;
    width: 31%;
    margin-right: 3.5%;
    padding: 1%;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    border-left: 2px solid #007700;
  }
  .box:last-child {
    margin-right: 0;
  }
  .clearfix::after {
    content: "";
    display: table;
    clear: both;
  }
  .footer {
    border-top: 2px solid #007700;
    padding-top: 1em;
    clear: both;
  }
</style>
...
<h1>Accessibility Layout Example</h1>
<h2>Fluid Design with Flexible Columns</h2>
<div class="wrapper clearfix">
  <div class="box" title="first section">
    <h3>Section A</h3>
    <p>
      This layout adjusts gracefully as text 
      grows or shrinks, making it suitable for 
      users who need to enlarge text without 
      layout issues.
    </p>
  </div>
  <div class="box" title="second section">
    <h3>Section B</h3>
    <p>
      The columns are defined with percentages 
      and floated left, allowing them to wrap 
      naturally if space becomes constrained.
    </p>
  </div>
  <div class="box" title="third section">
    <h3>Section C</h3>
    <p>
      For more advanced designs, consider using 
      modern CSS techniques such as Flexbox or 
      Grid, but this method remains widely 
      supported.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="footer">
  <p>End of layout demonstration.</p>
</div>
...

images_of_text.problem: This content uses images of text to convey information rather than actual text.
images_of_text.solution:
Solution 1

Add visible text next to the image that contains the same text as appears in the image. If the visual reading order is important, place the text in the same order. If the order does not matter for comprehension, ensure the text conveys the same meaning and information.

Solution 2

Remove the text from the image and use the text-free version as a CSS background image. Then add the same text as HTML content on top of the background image. Verify that the text maintains sufficient color contrast with the background to meet Success Criterion 1.4.3.

Solution 3

Use CSS to replace images of text with text and provide user interface controls to switch between them. To use this technique, create an HTML page that uses semantic elements to mark up the page structure. Then design two or more stylesheets for that page. One stylesheet presents the HTML text as text, and the second uses CSS features to replace some of the HTML text with images of text. Finally, use server-side or client-side scripting to provide a control that allows users to switch between the available views.
Code example:

HTML code example: 

<div id="header"> 
  <h1>
    <span>FutureTech Conference</span>
  </h1> 
  <h2>
    <span>Innovating Tomorrow's World</span>
  </h2> 
</div>
The CSS for the presentation that includes images of text: 
#header h1 {
  background-image: url(futuretech-logo.png);
  width: 300px;
  height: 100px;
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  margin-top: 0;
  position: absolute;
}
#header h1 span {
  position: absolute;
  left: -999em;
}
#header h2 {
  background-image: url(tagline.png);
  width: 280px;
  height: 50px;
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  margin-top: 120px;
  position: absolute;
}
#header h2 span {
  position: absolute;
  left: -999em;
}
The CSS for the presentation that does not include images of text: 
#header h1 {
  font: normal 180%/100% "Helvetica Neue", 
        sans-serif;
  color: #003366;
  background: #fff;
  margin: 0 0 0.5em 0;
}
#header h2 {
  font: normal 140%/100% "Helvetica Neue", 
        sans-serif;
  color: #006600;
  background: #fff;
  margin: 0;
}
